hook: Michael Dell began selling computers as a student at the University of Texas and founded the company that became Dell Technologies in 1984 with $1,000. He took it private with Silver Lake in 2013, bought EMC in 2016 and remains chairman and chief executive. Servers for AI are now a large part of the business, and the company reported a record $95 billion backlog of AI server orders at the end of its quarter to July 31, 2026.

quick_facts: Born in Houston, Texas, in 1965, he left the University of Texas at 19 to run his computer business full time.
In 1992 he became the youngest chief executive ever to earn a Fortune 500 ranking.
He stepped down as chief executive in 2004 while remaining chairman and took the role back on January 31, 2007.
The roughly $24.9 billion buyout that took Dell private with Silver Lake closed on October 29, 2013.
Dell completed its acquisition of EMC on September 7, 2016, forming Dell Technologies.
For the quarter ended July 31, 2026, Dell reported revenue of $47.0 billion, record AI server orders of $60.9 billion, AI server revenue of $16.4 billion and an AI server backlog of $95 billion.

achievements.title: Founder, Dell Technologies
achievements.impact: Built a company started in 1984 with $1,000 into one of the largest makers of computers and servers, and became the youngest CEO to earn a Fortune 500 ranking in 1992.

achievements.title: EMC acquisition
achievements.impact: Completed the purchase of EMC on September 7, 2016, bringing Dell EMC, VMware, Pivotal, RSA, SecureWorks and Virtustream into one group under the Dell Technologies name.

achievements.title: AI server business
achievements.impact: Dell booked a record $60.9 billion in AI server orders in the quarter to July 31, 2026, and ended it with a $95 billion AI server backlog.

achievements.title: Michael & Susan Dell Foundation
achievements.impact: Established the foundation with his wife in 1999 to fund work on health and education.

achievements.title: Bower Award for Business Leadership
achievements.impact: Received the Franklin Institute's award in 2013 for making personal computing more accessible.
